title: Guido van Rossum and the Coining of 'Benevolent Dictator for Life'
explainer: In 1995, on the early Python mailing list, core contributor Ken Manheimer proposed calling Guido van Rossum the project's 'Benevolent Dictator,' and fellow contributor Barry Warsaw added 'for Life' shortly after - a title that stuck for over two decades until van Rossum stepped back from it in 2018. The phrase names a real governance pattern you'll meet across upstream projects: a maintainer with final say on contested design calls, balanced by norms of open discussion and consensus for everything else. Recognizing that a project's BDFL or core-team model is a specific, named governance choice, not just 'whoever happens to be in charge,' changes how you read its contribution guidelines.

title: Richard Stallman's GNU Manifesto and the Ideology Behind 'Upstream' (1985)
explainer: When Richard Stallman published the GNU Manifesto in Dr. Dobb's Journal in March 1985, he wasn't just announcing a new operating system project; he was arguing that software users deserve the right to run, study, share, and modify the programs they depend on. That argument, and the Free Software Foundation he founded later that year to institutionalize it, is a large part of why upstream projects have contribution norms, licenses, and copyleft terms at all, rather than just a tree of unrelated private forks. Contributing to a language runtime today means operating inside expectations this manifesto did more than almost anything else to establish.
